problems.title: Serialisation
problems.statement: Count the serialised updates for one warp atomicAdd.

parts.prompt: All 32 lanes hit the same bin?
Lanes spread evenly over 4 bins (8 each)?
Every lane a different bin?

hints: The simulator charges the worst same-address count.
problems.solution: 32, 8 and 1. Contention, not the number of atomics, sets the cost.

problems.title: Privatisation

parts.prompt: Global atomics, naive (one per pixel)?
Global atomics with per-block shared histograms, at most?

hints: Each block merges each non-zero bin once.
problems.solution: (a) 1,048,576. (b) 16,384: 64× fewer, and the per-pixel atomics now run in shared memory.

problems.title: Random bins
problems.statement: 32 lanes pick bins independently and uniformly from 256.

parts.prompt: Expected largest number of lanes on one bin (the serialisation)?

hints: $E[\max] = \sum_{k \ge 1} P(\max \ge k)$; compute $P(\max \le k)$ exactly or estimate the birthday-style collisions.
problems.solution: $1.94$. The probability of any collision is high ($1 - \prod_{i<32}(1 - i/256) \approx 87\%$), but triple collisions are rare, so a warp on uniform data costs about 2 passes. Skewed data is what hurts.

problems.title: A skewed image
problems.statement: 60% of pixels are 0 (as in Lab 3); the rest are spread over other values. Lanes are independent.

parts.prompt: Expected lanes per warp on bin 0?
Probability that all 32 lanes are 0?

problems.solution: (a) $32 \times 0.6 = 19.2$: the serialisation is about 19–20 per warp atomic, about 10× the uniform case. (b) $7.96e-08$: warps are almost never uniform, so the expensive case is the common case.

problems.title: Warp aggregation
problems.statement: Using __match_any_sync (or ballots), each group of lanes with equal values elects a leader, which adds the group's size with one atomic.

parts.prompt: Atomics per warp on a constant image?
On a warp with 5 distinct values?
Worst case?

problems.solution: 1, 5 and 32 (all different, where aggregation only adds overhead). Aggregation targets exactly the skewed case that privatisation can't fix.

problems.title: Counting runs locally
problems.statement: Each thread processes 16 consecutive pixels and does one atomic per run of equal values.

parts.prompt: Atomics per thread in a constant region?
On pixels that alternate between two values?

hints: A run ends when the value changes.
problems.solution: 1 and 16. Real images have long runs (sky, background), so this simple trick removes most of the contention, at the cost of uncoalesced per-thread chunks unless the data is staged through shared memory.

problems.title: Compare-and-swap loops
problems.statement: c threads simultaneously run a CAS loop on the same address; each round exactly one succeeds and the others retry.

parts.prompt: Total CAS attempts for c = 32?
Rounds until the last one succeeds?

problems.solution: $32 + 31 + \dots + 1 = 528$ attempts over 32 rounds: quadratic. Native atomics (atomicAdd, atomicMax) are far better than CAS loops whenever they exist.

problems.title: Allocating output slots
problems.statement: $10^6$ threads each append one item to a queue with atomicAdd(count, 1).

parts.prompt: Atomics on the counter?
With warp aggregation (one atomic per warp, lanes take base + rank)?

problems.solution: (a) $10^6$ atomics on one address, all serialised at L2. (b) 31,250. Compilers now do this aggregation automatically for the simple case.

problems.title: Float atomics

parts.prompt: Which are true?
options: The result can differ between runs in the last bits
The result is always within a few ulps of the exact sum regardless of n
Changing the grid size can change the result

hints: Order of additions depends on timing.
problems.solution: Each atomic is indivisible, but the sequence order isn't fixed, so the rounding differs between runs and with grid size. The error is that of some sequential sum: it grows with n, not bounded by a few ulps.

problems.title: Per-warp sub-histograms
problems.statement: A block keeps one 256-bin histogram per warp (8 warps) in shared memory instead of one per block.

parts.prompt: Shared memory used, in bytes (4-byte bins)?
On a constant image, the serialisation per warp atomic is…

hints: Which collisions do per-warp copies remove?
problems.solution: 8 KB. Per-warp copies stop warps from colliding with each other (fewer cross-warp conflicts at the same counters), but lanes of one warp still hit the same counter: 32. Inside a warp, you need aggregation or run counting.
